tabs.title: Understanding the message
tabs.description: Interpret the writer's purpose and feelings.

tabs.title: Responding appropriately
tabs.description: Apply the author's ideas to a new situation.

questions.q: What is the implication of Elias calling his explanation of limited time 'conveniently incomplete'?
choices: He cannot remember the order of his journeys.
His professional busyness disguises how actively he chose polished public updates over honest correspondence.
His old friend has unfairly exaggerated the length of their silence.
His job requires him to conceal all personal experiences.
questions.explanation: He admits having ample time for curated updates while failing to offer real personal availability.

questions.q: Why does the dockworker's rejection of the phrase 'close-knit community' matter to the museum's work?
choices: It shows that all oral-history interviews should be anonymous.
It demonstrates that local communities never offer mutual assistance.
It proves that the museum should avoid discussing difficult memories.
It challenges a comforting narrative by preserving both solidarity and resentment.
questions.explanation: The dockworker describes mutual help under necessity, not uncomplicated community harmony.

questions.q: What distinguishes the father's postcards from Elias's own carefully composed updates?
choices: The postcards contained more detailed information about daily life.
The postcards made up for every absence during the daughter's childhood.
Their limited claims honestly signalled attention without pretending to repair what was missing.
They were sent more frequently than Elias's modern messages.
questions.explanation: The daughter values modest signs of life while refusing to romanticise the father's absence.

questions.q: What does Elias mean by the risk of an invitation acquiring an 'invisible invoice'?
choices: A generous-sounding gesture may carry an unspoken demand for emotional repayment.
The museum might charge guests unexpected admission costs.
An invitation can be accepted only after travel expenses are reimbursed.
A public event may require additional staff to keep accounts.
questions.explanation: Elias fears making friendship transactional by treating attendance or refusal as evidence of loyalty.

questions.q: Why does the writer suggest that listening sometimes means giving up the pleasure of being useful?
choices: He believes practical help is always disrespectful.
Offering tidy solutions can overwrite complex experiences that deserve to be heard on their own terms.
He thinks interviews become successful only when contributors agree with the curator.
The museum has stopped presenting stories of community support.
questions.explanation: The archive experience shows that correction and complexity may require restraint instead of fixing a story.

questions.q: Why would an extensive confession risk transferring emotional labour to Amara?
choices: It would reveal information she had already read online.
It would force Amara to attend the museum's opening ceremony.
It might oblige her to reassure Elias about his moral worth rather than respond freely.
It would make the invitation impossible to understand.
questions.explanation: Elias explicitly refuses to seek reassurance that he is still a decent friend.

questions.q: What does the closing promise to resist treating Amara's response as a 'verdict' chiefly establish?
choices: Elias expects Amara to answer positively after reading the letter.
He believes the earlier friendship can be reconstructed exactly.
He intends to withdraw the invitation if she appears uncertain.
Her answer should not become a judgement on his identity or a test of her loyalty.
questions.explanation: The conclusion seeks a relationship that accommodates changed people and free responses.

questions.q: A museum editor wants to remove a contributor's difficult memories to create a reassuring ending. What response follows Elias's reasoning?
choices: Accept the edit because inspiration matters more than accuracy.
Retain the tensions if they better reflect the person's lived experience.
Replace the contributor's words with an approved community summary.
Ask the contributor to change their account to sound more positive.
questions.explanation: Elias values the museum leaving the dockworker's contradiction intact rather than polishing it away.

questions.q: Amara declines the listening-room event but proposes exchanging letters slowly. What response most respects the letter?
choices: Welcome the alternative without requiring a rapid reply or explanation.
Ask for a firm future attendance commitment before continuing contact.
Explain that correspondence counts only after a face-to-face meeting.
Interpret her refusal as evidence against her sincerity.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph proposes unhurried correspondence as a legitimate form of renewed contact.

questions.q: Which description best captures the ethical ambition of Elias's invitation?
choices: To demonstrate sincerity through a sufficiently detailed apology.
To secure an audience for the museum's opening while avoiding criticism.
To recreate their past friendship through a memorable public event.
To offer contact without coercing a particular response or demanding reassurance.
questions.explanation: Elias openly recognises potentially instrumental motives and refuses to punish a refusal or demand emotional validation.
